questions.prompt: What does spread spectrum do to a radio signal?
options: Squeezes it into the narrowest band possible
Spreads it over a much wider band than it needs, using a code both ends know
Encrypts it with AES
Splits it into IP packets

questions.prompt: Spread spectrum changes the physical radio signal itself. Which OSI layer is that? (a number)
In DSSS, what happens to each data bit?
options: It's sent on a different frequency each time
It's replaced by a fast pattern of chips, the chipping code
It gets its own time slot
It's repeated until the receiver acknowledges it

questions.prompt: With DSSS, a receiver can still recover a bit even if noise flips a few of its chips.
Why does FHSS resist eavesdropping and jamming?
options: It only works over cables
It hops between narrow channels in a pseudo-random order that only the two ends know
It transmits at much higher power
It encrypts every hop with WPA3

questions.prompt: Classic Bluetooth hops across how many channels? (a number)
A jammer blasts noise on one frequency. Which radio suffers least?
options: A narrowband radio fixed on that frequency
Both suffer equally
An FHSS radio hopping across 79 channels
Neither, because jamming is impossible

options: Circuit switching and message switching
Time slots, and hopping between carrier frequencies
CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA
SSIDs and beacons
